archetype.name: Fallen Contender (lost season)
archetype.definition: A team with recent 14-win and 11-win pedigree whose underlying play has bottomed out across the board, leaving a roster that grades as the league's worst while the brand still looks like a contender.

report.headline: A year after 11 wins, the Eagles grade out as the league's worst team
report.take:
This is not a good team having a bad run. By net EPA the Eagles are 32nd of 32, with the offense 29th and the defense 27th. That is a long way from 2024, when they ranked 3rd in net EPA and went 14-3, and from last year's 11-win team that was still 8th. The last time a Philadelphia season looked like this was 2020, and even that team had a top-half defense by EPA. This one has no unit carrying the other.

The 2-0 start was thinner than it looked. They beat Washington and Tennessee as 6- and 7-point favorites and failed to cover either. They have lost six straight since, and the recent losses are the ugliest: 21-38 to Dallas and 10-27 at Washington. The offense can't stay on schedule. Its success rate is 31st, it gains 265.1 yards a game (31st), and the run game is stuffed at the line more often than anyone's. The quarterback spot has also flipped, with Tanner McKee starting Weeks 6 and 8 around Jalen Hurts, and neither version has produced positive passing EPA in a game since Week 2. The defense can't make a negative play. Pressure rate is 27th, QB hit rate dead last, and takeaways 31st. So drives against them end only when the opponent ends them.

Two things the record hides point in opposite directions. Wins over expected is -1.4, and the point differential implies 3.4 wins rather than 2, so a little bad luck is baked into the standings. But the differential itself is being propped up by special teams that rank 6th in EPA per game, while the offense and defense are both bottom-five by EPA. The 0.143 cover rate, 31st, says the market has kept overrating them all year. If anything, the efficiency says the point differential flatters them.

The path forward is mostly about health and the quarterback. The receiving corps is gutted this week, with DeVonta Smith and Dontayvion Wicks out. The cornerback room is down to its third and fourth options, and the lead backup back, Dameon Pierce, is on IR. With a run defense 31st in EPA and a pass rush that can't get home, there is no obvious lever that turns this around quickly. The realistic goal is stealing games against the softer back half of the schedule, not a playoff push.

strengths.title: Special teams winning hidden yardage
strengths.body: The kicking and return units are the only phase grading as clearly above average, 6th in EPA per game. That is why the point differential looks less dire than the efficiency numbers. It is real and fairly stable, but it is the smallest lever in football and can't cover for two bottom-five units every week.

strengths.title: Coverage holds outside the top target
strengths.body: The secondary has kept opponents' second and third receivers and tight ends under their usual output. The damage comes almost entirely through the WR1. That reads as a scheme that brackets well but has no corner who can win one-on-one. With three corners now out or questionable, even this piece is at risk.

strengths.title: Aggression on fourth down
strengths.body: Sirianni's staff goes for it at the league's highest rate in its decision spots. For an offense this inefficient, extra possessions and shortened fields are the right bet. Pairing that aggression with a 31st-ranked success rate means it will produce as many turnovers on downs as it saves drives.

concerns.title: No pass rush, no takeaways
concerns.body: The defense is 27th in pressure rate, last in QB hit rate, and 31st in takeaways. Quarterbacks get comfortable pockets and drives don't end early. This is a personnel problem rather than variance: the sack total sits 30th and has been low in every game. Without it, the defense has no way to manufacture short fields for a struggling offense.

concerns.title: The run game dies at the line
concerns.body: Eagles backs are stuffed at a league-worst rate and get 2.09 yards before contact (28th). That points at the line rather than the backs. It strips away the offense's old identity and leaves whichever quarterback is playing in long down-and-distances behind a front allowing the 27th-ranked pressure rate. The 22- and 35-yard rushing games against Jacksonville and Carolina show how low the floor is.

concerns.title: Soft run defense, poor tackling
concerns.body: Opponents run on them with success: 31st in rush EPA allowed, with missed tackles 30th. The lead back facing them has posted the league's best EPA per play. That makes them easy to play against with a lead and lets opponents bleed the clock, which helps explain why Philadelphia is 31st in time of possession.

trend.note: Two narrow wins to open, then six straight losses. The last two, to Dallas and Washington, were the most lopsided, and the only cover of the season came in Week 5.

nextGame.headline: Run-heavy Giants aim straight at the Eagles' softest spot
nextGame.body:
New York is a team whose record outruns its play. At 4-2-1 it is only 16th in net EPA, with the league's 3rd-best luck by wins over expected and a 0.714 cover rate that leads the league. Its identity is ball control: 30th in pass rate over expected and 2nd in time of possession. That is exactly the shape that exploits an Eagles defense 31st against the run and 31st in time of possession itself. The opening for Philadelphia is on the other side. The Giants' pass rush is the league's weakest by pressure rate, they allow red-zone touchdowns at the 28th-ranked rate, and they give up explosive runs often (28th). The Book has the Giants by 3.5 on the road with a 40.5 total.

Availability tilts against Philadelphia. DeVonta Smith and Dontayvion Wicks are out, so the targets fall to Makai Lemon, Dallas Goedert and Darius Cooper. Linebacker Jihaad Campbell is out, and the corner room is down with Jonathan Jones out, Jakorian Bennett on IR and Michael Carter II questionable. Who starts at quarterback isn't settled in the dossier after McKee started last week. The Giants have their own holes: linebacker Tremaine Edmunds on IR, safety Jevon Holland and corner Greg Newsome II questionable with concussions, and a backfield thinned by Tyrone Tracy Jr.'s IR stint with Cam Skattebo day-to-day. A diminished Giants run game would take away their cleanest edge.

waysToWin.title: Clean pockets against a passive rush
waysToWin.body: The Giants generate the league's lowest pressure rate, a rare chance for an Eagles line that has struggled in protection. Even with depleted receivers, time to work the intermediate game and lean on Goedert keeps drives alive. Their deep defense is stingy, so this has to be patient rather than explosive.

waysToWin.title: Finish drives in the red zone
waysToWin.body: New York concedes touchdowns on 0.778 of red-zone trips, 28th. Paired with Philadelphia's go-for-it habit on fourth down, a few extended drives can turn into sevens instead of field goals. That is how a weak offense keeps pace in a low-total game.

waysToWin.title: Hidden yards on special teams
waysToWin.body: Philadelphia's special teams rate well ahead of New York's by EPA per game. In a game projected around 40 points, a field-position edge or a return can be the margin. It is the one phase where the Eagles are clearly the better side.

waysToLose.title: Giants grind them out on the ground
waysToLose.body: New York runs far more than expected and holds the ball longer than all but one team. The Eagles' run defense ranks 31st in EPA and misses tackles. If the Giants' backfield is healthy enough, long drives shorten the game and starve an offense that can't afford fewer possessions.

waysToLose.title: Depleted receivers meet stingy coverage
waysToLose.body: With Smith and Wicks out, the passing game runs through Lemon and Goedert. New York ranks 4th in EPA allowed to both the WR1 and the TE1. If those two are taken away, there is little else to throw to, and the 31st-ranked success rate stalls drives.

waysToLose.title: Can't punish a sack-prone line
waysToLose.body: The Giants allow sacks at the 26th-ranked rate, an obvious target. But Philadelphia's sack rate is last in the league, so the mismatch probably goes unused. Without negative plays, New York stays on schedule and protects a lead.

nextGame.watch: Whether the Eagles can stop the Giants' early-down runs. If New York controls the clock as it has all year, Philadelphia's thin offense gets too few possessions to overcome it.

restOfSeason.body:
Expect more of the same with some modest point-differential improvement rather than a turnaround. The bad luck in close games, wins over expected of -1.4, should even out a bit. The back half also includes softer spots: Indianapolis and Houston at home, and a Dallas defense ranked 32nd. But the core problems are structural, not random: a line that can't open runs, a pass rush that doesn't exist, and a run defense near the bottom. Those don't regress toward the mean on their own, and Pittsburgh, Seattle and San Francisco still loom.

What's sustainable is the special-teams edge and the fourth-down aggression. What's fragile is everything that depends on health. Getting Smith and Wicks back and settling on a quarterback would lift the offense from bottom-three toward bottom-ten. A secondary down multiple corners could make the defense worse before it gets better. A finish in the four-to-six-win range is the realistic band.
swingFactors: Hurts' availability and who starts at QB
Smith and Wicks returning to the receiving corps
Cornerback health with three corners hurt

confidence.note: Eight games is a real sample and the EPA picture is consistent, but QB flux and heavy injuries cloud the outlook.
